newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African massacre mystery remains after trial.
newsitem.headline: S.African massacre mystery remains after trial.

text.p: The acquittal of former defence minister Magnus Malan on Friday has frustrated South Africans who believe a hidden white hand was behind a decade of political violence between blacks in KwaZulu-Natal province.

The 1987 KwaMakutha massacre for which Malan was charged was one of countless such attacks, but it was singled out as a test case to see if state leaders could be held responsible for politically motivated atrocities committed while they were in power.
The answer in this case was No.

More than 14,000 people have been killed in KwaZulu-Natal province since the mid-1980s when violence erupted between Mangosuthu Buthelezi's Inkatha Freedom Party and the African National Congress of current President Nelson Mandela.
ANC leaders from Mandela down regularly blamed the violence on a "third force" comprising members of the white security establishment.

Judge Jan Hugo said it had been proven that Inkatha gunmen trained by the white government were to blame for KwaMakutha, in which 13 people, including six children, were killed in the house of an ANC sympathiser.
"There can be little doubt that the KwaMakutha victims were gunned down by Inkatha trainees," he said.

Malan had endorsed a secret military plan to train 206 Zulus at the request of Inkatha leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi to defend his nominally independent KwaZulu homeland government against his fiercest rival, the ANC.
But the judge found that the state had failed to prove that Malan and his fellow white officers were guilty of the murders.
After the acquittals, Mandela vowed that investigations into who was responsible for KwaMakutha and other apartheid-era crimes would continue.

"We give the assurance that where persons have died as a result of atrocities, we will continue to investigate who was responsible and who, in regard to alleged third force activities, was responsible for directing these activities."
